claims.text: Configurational entropy alone does not govern the intrinsic thermal stability of nearly equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
HENA stability depends critically on surface-energy minimization, synthesis-induced kinetic trapping, and element-specific diffusion activation barriers.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of HENAs creates a driving force for phase or surface segregation that competes with entropy stabilization.
CoNiCuRuPd and FeCoPdIrPt are examples of five-component HEA nanoparticle systems.
CoNiCuRuPd and FeCoPdIrPt have sufficiently similar atomic radii and cohesive energies to favor metastable single-phase structures.
The elevated-temperature single-phase state of these HENAs exists only because diffusion activation energies are significantly greater than the available thermal energy.
Rapid thermal synthesis methods can produce multielement HEA nanoparticles while suppressing phase separation.
The cited CoNiCuRuPd and FeCoPdIrPt particles are homogeneous, single-phase FCC nanoparticles with diameters of 2-5 nm.
At low temperature, high diffusion barriers prevent atomic rearrangement and kinetically preserve a single-phase structure despite a thermodynamic driving force for segregation.
Increasing temperature activates atomic diffusion and permits the nanoparticles to approach lower-total-free-energy structures.
Elements with lower surface energies will preferentially segregate to nanoparticle surfaces.
The nanoparticle interior favors phase separation when doing so reduces the enthalpy of mixing.
For 2-5 nm particles, a critical transition temperature of approximately 700-800 K separates a minimally segregated regime from rapid segregation.
Above the critical temperature, segregation will produce core-shell structures or decomposition into elemental phases.
The segregation rate will depend strongly on elemental composition and element-specific diffusion barriers.
Particles smaller than 2 nm will have a narrower thermal-stability window because surface-energy contributions are larger.
Large constituent-size asymmetry promotes rapid diffusion of smaller atoms and places the proposed model outside its valid boundary.
Particles smaller than 1 nm fall outside the model because surface effects dominate completely.
Reactive species such as hydrogen can lower diffusion barriers and invalidate the proposed stability model.
Kinetic trapping as the primary stability mechanism would be falsified if particles remain stable to 1000 K regardless of size or segregate immediately without a size-dependent transition threshold.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts decomposition below 2 nm, which includes particles below 1 nm, while the boundary field states that the model fails below 1 nm. The prediction therefore extends into a range explicitly excluded from the model.

Hydrogen is specified as a regular annealing environment, but reactive hydrogen is also identified as a condition that may lower diffusion barriers and invalidate the model. Results obtained under H2 would therefore not cleanly test the stated intrinsic kinetic-stability mechanism without a separate Ar comparison.
